newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn cool on Franco-Spanish Zaire force proposal.
newsitem.headline: Bonn cool on Franco-Spanish Zaire force proposal.

text.p: Germany gave a cool response on Thursday to a Franco-Spanish proposal to send troops to aid refugees caught in ethnic conflict in Zaire, saying the task was one for African nations.
"At the moment it is completely open who would take part in such a force," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told parliament in a statement.

He drew attention to the outcome of Tuesday's African summit in Nairobi which called for the urgent deployment of a neutral force to protect the refugees, hundreds of thousands of whom are in danger from thirst and starvation.
"Primarily this would be the task of the Organisation of African Unity," he said.

At the same time, Kinkel said he feared there would not be a "purely African solution" to the crisis. He said Bonn was "prepared to start up immediate humanitarian help as soon as the situation on the ground allows".

He noted Germany had put a draft resolution to the United Nations Security Council which proposed an immediate ceasefire, the establishment of safe corridors to let relief supplies through, and a regional security conference.
"The international community must leave no stone unturned to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe," he said.
He added that Germany, for 30 years a colonial power in neighbouring Burundi and Rwanda, had successfully urged a reluctant Rwanda to attend the Nairobi summit.

But Kinkel said he had failed to get South African President Nelson Mandela to mediate in the conflict. Nevertheless, a Zairean envoy said in Johannesburg on Thursday that Mandela had promised to play a major diplomatic role in peace efforts.

More than a million refugees have been displaced by the conflict in eastern Zaire involving Zairean ethnic Tutsis, Zairean government forces and Rwandan Hutu refugees already displaced from their homeland.

A Spanish foreign ministry spokesman said on Wednesday that Spain and France wanted to send a force of at least 5,000 soldiers to Zaire to ensure security for aid distribution, but would not go ahead unless the United States and U.N. backed it.
European Union development ministers meeting in Brussels on Thursday issued a declaration that they were ready to act in any way necessary.
But they did not back the Franco-Spanish plan and failed to produce any new ideas on how to deal with the deteriorating situation beyond sending a new fact-finding team to the area.
